strengths: Novel meta-AFA problem formulation addressing retrospective missingness with sound theoretical foundations (Theorems 3.4, 4.2)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (GP, MiniBooNE, MNIST, Metabric, MIMIC-IV) with systematic study of varying context lengths and missingness rates
Improved uncertainty quantification demonstrated consistently (Figures 3, 7) with better calibration than task-specific baselines, particularly as features accumulate
Elegant in-context learning approach eliminating per-task retraining, offering practical computational savings
Honest and rigorous experimental reporting with good acknowledgment of limitations and ablation studies showing when adaptivity helps/hurts
Strong reproducibility with comprehensive hyperparameters, detailed experimental setup, promised code release, and adequate documentation
weaknesses: Limited real-world empirical gains: Performance on real datasets (MIMIC, Metabric) shows marginal improvements or performance indistinguishable from baselines (Figures 8-9); adaptivity sometimes provides no benefit (Fig 13)

Restrictive and unverifiable assumptions: MAR is untestable; blocked policies prevent generalization to tasks with different missingness patterns; positivity/sufficient coverage is vague with no practical verification methods or robustness analysis

Scalability limitations: Only evaluated on small feature sets (≤20 features); no high-dimensional experiments; computational cost of L2M vs baselines not compared; DQN excluded from synthetic tasks due to computational constraints

Semi-synthetic evaluation introduces distribution shift: BNN priors for training + real labels for testing limits confidence in transfer; paper acknowledges performance 'depends on alignment' but doesn't systematically characterize when transfer succeeds/fails

Technical gaps: Gumbel-Softmax bias impact not quantified; surrogate loss optimality relies on Covert et al.'s practical heuristic rather than principled approximation; sequence model approximates Bayesian inference via inductive biases—a still-debated connection

Missing critical analyses: No failure mode investigation; no ablations on architecture choices; no investigation of learned patterns; no computational time comparisons; blocked policy constraint not discussed as potential limitation for generalization

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with explicit treatment of retrospective missingness, addressing a practically important limitation of existing AFA methods
Solid theoretical contributions including identifiability of CMI under missingness (Theorem 3.4) and optimality guarantees for sequence loss objective (Theorem 4.2)
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (synthetic, semi-synthetic, real) with multiple evaluation metrics showing robustness to limited labeled data and high missingness rates
Avoids expensive posterior sampling through sequence modeling, providing practical scalability advantages over prior generative modeling approaches
Honest and thorough discussion of limitations with extensive ablations and stress tests in appendix
weaknesses: Significant gap between theory and practice: Theorem 4.2 assumes perfect optimization, but implementation uses biased gradient estimator (straight-through Gumbel-softmax); Figure 17 shows non-negligible bias but impact on theoretical guarantees not characterized

Greedy policies fundamentally limited for jointly informative features (acknowledged in Appendix A.4 but deserves more prominence); lookahead variant shows only modest improvements (Figure 5) while increasing computational cost

Strong, unverifiable assumptions (MAR, Positivity, No Direct Effect) with no practical diagnostics for violations; Positivity especially problematic—requires sufficient data coverage of each feature action, easily violated in practice

Limited practical improvements on real data: Figure 8 shows mixed results with overlapping confidence intervals; MIMIC improvements are modest (~0.02 NLL); Figure 14 shows fully synthetic pretraining requires task-specific fine-tuning, undermining efficiency claims

Proof-of-concept status limits impact: Authors acknowledge lack of deployment readiness, scalability undemonstrated, semi-synthetic evaluation may not reflect realistic scenarios, and no evidence of clinical utility/interpretability important for healthcare deployment

Methodological concerns: baseline modifications (fixed vs. decay schedules) may not represent methods at their best; DQN excluded from synthetic tasks; potential domain shift from semi-synthetic pretraining to real test labels

Technical contributions are incremental: combines existing techniques (sequence models for uncertainty, CMI selection, Gumbel-softmax) rather than novel algorithms; builds directly on recent sequence-modeling-for-Bayesian-inference work
